fields.sample_size: fieldwork in Kisumu (KIWASCO) and Nakuru (NAWASSCO), Kenya, in three phases (January-April 2017, January-April 2018, April-June 2019): field observation, document and report review and semi-structured interviews with 78 key respondents (utility staff, water point operators and residents, NGO, bilateral and multilateral agency and government staff including WASREB and the Water Sector Trust Fund, and suppliers of pre-paid dispensers, PPDs)
fields.effect_measure: qualitative case-study analysis (pragmatism framework) of utility decision-making; no quantitative estimate
fields.effect_estimate: Kenyan utilities have a mixed mandate under the Water Act 2002 (operate on a commercial basis while delivering universal access under the 2010 Constitution right to clean and safe water); in low-income areas they serve through intermediaries (kiosks, yard taps resold by landlords, delegated management models). KIWASCO supplies about 450,000 people (about 60% in low-income areas), serves six of 22 low-income areas through delegated management with 39 master operators and 340 kiosks; Nakuru installed its first 15 pre-paid dispensers in 2012 (compounds of 6-10 households, financed by the Water Services Trust Fund) after success stories at provider-association meetings and donor funding was available; PPD water is sold at the official price of Ksh 1 (Kisumu) or Ksh 1.5 (Nakuru), below the kiosk price. The authors show that managers adopted PPDs as a pragmatic, contextually best-available option, with limits (landlord and consumer unwillingness to invest, breakdowns, affordability) and argue pragmatism works only combined with advocacy and ideology-informed approaches.
